objectives: Never trust figure scale; solve from given relationships
Use similar triangles and the special-right-triangle ratios
Apply SOH-CAH-TOA and the sine/cosine cofunction identity

slides.title: Part 1 — The most formula-driven domain
slides.body: Geometry & Trigonometry (~15% of Math) rewards a compact, memorized relationship set and one iron rule: never trust how a figure *looks*.

slides.title: What it tests
slides.body:
- **Lines & angles:** vertical, supplementary/complementary, parallel-line angle pairs.
- **Triangles:** angle-sum 180°, similarity, Pythagorean theorem, the special right triangles (45-45-90, 30-60-90), the common Pythagorean triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13).
- **Circles:** area, circumference, arc length, sector area, central vs inscribed angles.
- **Area & volume** of standard solids.
- **Right-triangle trig:** SOH-CAH-TOA; the sine/cosine cofunction identity; basic radian sense.

Most items are a one- or two-step application of a known relationship — *if* you don't get baited by the picture.

slides.title: The rule that prevents the biggest trap
slides.body:
> **Figures are NOT drawn to scale unless explicitly stated.** Never measure, eyeball, or assume from appearance — solve only from given/derivable relationships.

The SAT deliberately distorts figures so the visually 'obvious' answer is a wrong choice. Trust marked values, given equalities, and theorems; treat the drawing as a *topology sketch*, not a measurement. This single discipline prevents the most common geometry error.

slides.title: Part 2 — Strategy a top scorer uses
Similar triangles are everywhere
slides.body: Equal angles ⇒ **similar** triangles ⇒ **proportional** sides. A large share of SAT geometry is "spot the similar triangles, write the side proportion." Triggers: shared angles, parallel lines cutting a triangle, an altitude to the hypotenuse. The instant you see equal angles, set up $\dfrac{a}{a'}=\dfrac{b}{b'}$ — the rest is algebra.

slides.title: SOH-CAH-TOA and the cofunction identity
slides.body: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{opp}{hyp},\ \cos\theta=\dfrac{adj}{hyp},\ \tan\theta=\dfrac{opp}{adj}$. SAT favorite: the **cofunction identity** $\sin\theta=\cos(90^\circ-\theta)$ — complementary angles swap sine and cosine. Recognizing it converts an apparently hard trig item ("if $\sin x=0.6$, find $\cos(90^\circ-x)$") into one line ($=0.6$).

slides.title: Part 3 — Method: special right triangle, derived

question.question: Derive the 45-45-90 side ratio
question.goal: Show that an isosceles right triangle has sides in ratio $1:1:\sqrt{2}$.

steps.prompt: A 45-45-90 triangle has two equal legs. Call each leg length 1. The two acute angles are equal — why must the two legs be equal?
steps.motivation: Equal base angles ⇒ isosceles ⇒ the sides opposite them (the legs) are equal.

options: Equal angles are opposite equal sides (isosceles)
Right triangles always have equal legs

hints: What does 'equal base angles' imply about opposite sides?
steps.reveal: Equal angles ⇒ equal opposite sides ⇒ the legs are equal (length 1 each).

steps.prompt: Apply the Pythagorean theorem with legs 1 and 1. The hypotenuse h satisfies h² = ?
steps.motivation: a² + b² = c² with a = b = 1.
Take the positive square root (a length).

steps.prompt: Why can you reuse this ratio for ANY 45-45-90 triangle, not just legs of length 1?
steps.motivation: All 45-45-90 triangles are similar, so corresponding sides are proportional — the ratio is scale-invariant.

rubricCriteria.description: similar triangles have proportional sides, so the ratio 1:1:√2 scales to any size

hints: What do equal angles guarantee about two triangles?
steps.reveal: Same angles ⇒ all 45-45-90 triangles are similar ⇒ sides always in 1:1:√2, any scale.

slides.title: Part 4 — Worked examples, end to end
Worked example 1 — Pythagorean / triples
slides.body: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8; find the hypotenuse. $c^2=6^2+8^2=36+64=100\Rightarrow c=10$. Faster: recognize 6-8-10 as the 3-4-5 triple scaled by 2 — memorizing 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 lets you skip the arithmetic entirely on many items.

question.question: c² = 100, so c = ____.
question.explanation: √100 = 10 (the 6-8-10 triangle is just a scaled 3-4-5 — memorizing 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 saves time).

question.question: On the SAT, if a figure 'looks' isosceles but no equal sides/angles are marked, you should:
options: Not assume it — use only given/derivable information
Measure it with your answer sheet
Pick the answer that matches the picture
question.explanation: Figures aren't to scale unless stated. Visual assumptions are the intended trap; rely on marked information and theorems.

slides.title: Worked example 2 — special right triangle
slides.body: "A 30-60-90 triangle has short leg 5; find the hypotenuse." 30-60-90 sides are in ratio $1:\sqrt3:2$ (short leg : long leg : hypotenuse). Short leg corresponds to '1', so scale factor = 5; hypotenuse $=2\times5=10$. The trap choice $5\sqrt3$ is the *long* leg — the test offers the other side as bait. Know which ratio slot is which.

slides.title: The geometry trap families
slides.body:
1. **Eyeball-the-figure** — assuming a length/angle/right-angle that isn't marked (figures not to scale).
2. **Radius vs diameter** — using $d$ where $r$ belongs; in $A=\pi r^2$ that's a **4×** error, and the wrong value is offered.
3. **Wrong ratio slot** — in 30-60-90, returning the long leg ($\sqrt3$) when the hypotenuse (2) was asked.
4. **Unit/area-vs-perimeter** mix-ups.

Marked-info-only, extract-the-radius-first, label-the-ratio-slots: that defeats the bait.

question.question: Diagnose the mistake.
question.scenario: A student computes a circle's area with the diameter instead of the radius, getting an answer 4× too big — and it matches one of the choices.

rubricCriteria.description: A = πr², and r = d/2 — using d for r squares the error (factor 4)
the SAT seeds the 'used diameter' value as a distractor
fix: extract the radius first, label it, then substitute

question.explanation: Circle formulas use the *radius*. Plugging the diameter into πr² scales the area by 4 — and that wrong value is deliberately offered as a choice.

slides.workedSolution: 30-60-90 ⇒ sides 1:√3:2 with the short leg as '1'. Short leg 5 ⇒ scale ×5 ⇒ hypotenuse = 2×5 = 10. 5√3 is the *long leg* (the seeded trap).

question.question: In a 30-60-90 triangle the short leg is 5. The hypotenuse is:
question.explanation: 30-60-90 sides are in ratio 1 : √3 : 2 (short leg : long leg : hypotenuse). Hypotenuse = 2 × short leg = 10.

question.question: A circle has radius 3. Its area is ____ (use π, e.g. 9pi).
question.explanation: A = πr² = π(3)² = 9π. Use the radius, never the diameter.

question.prompt: Teach back: why is 'the figure is not to scale' the single most important sentence on SAT geometry?

rubricCriteria.description: the SAT distorts figures so the visually obvious answer is wrong
solutions must use marked values + theorems, never measurement
eyeballing is the intended, seeded trap

question.question: Give the two special-right-triangle ratios and one situation where each saves time.

rubricCriteria.description: ties each to a quick example/use

slides.title: How it scores & what's next
slides.body: That completes all 8 SAT domains at model depth. You've trained the verbal *and* math skills with strategy, derivations, multiple worked examples, and trap taxonomies. The SAT-prep path's **capstone** is the full timed exam — sit it under real conditions to convert these skills into a score.
